answer:
Hypothesis (data-grounded, answering "Does increased time preference lead to higher BMI?"):

The NLSY79 data provide weak evidence for a positive association between present-oriented (time-preferring) behavior and BMI, but do not support a causal claim. Using baseline BMI from 1981 weight (pounds) and 1985 height (inches; 4-year cross-pairing, n=10,573) and 1989 savings behavior as a proxy for time preference (net withdrawal from savings = present-oriented vs. net deposit = future-oriented; n=5,469 in the main model), individuals who took more money out of savings in 1989 had a higher baseline BMI in 1981 than those who put more money in: +0.28 kg/m² (95% CI 0.10–0.46, ≈0.08 SD) after adjusting for sex, age, race/ethnicity, family income, and education. The gradient is monotonic across all four savings categories (deposit 22.28 < no change 22.54 < withdrawal 22.56 < no savings 22.85) and is robust to a 4-level ordinal measure (+0.11 per step), continuous signed log net savings (more savings, lower BMI), weight winsorization, and adding a cognitive (ASVAB) covariate; the association with obesity (BMI≥30) is positive but not significant (OR 1.16, 95% CI 0.88–1.55) and is driven mainly by women. Because BMI was measured in 1981—before the 1989 savings behavior—this finding must be read as a cross-person association: individuals exhibiting more present-oriented saving behavior in 1989 had higher baseline BMI in 1981. Reverse causation (baseline BMI/health status shaping later saving choices) cannot be ruled out, so the hypothesis that increased time preference leads to higher BMI is, at most, weakly supported as an association and not established as causal in this data.

Workflow: (1) Data QC of nls_raw.csv (n=12,686): missingness audit, unit validation (weights identified as pounds, Height-1985 as inches, Height-1981 flagged as corrupted), outlier screening; (2) Constructed BMI = W1981(lb)×0.453592 / (H1985(in)×0.0254)²; (3) Operationalized time preference three ways—binary (net withdrawal vs net deposit), 4-level ordinal, and signed log net savings; (4) Descriptive group means by sex, univariate t-test/point-biserial/Spearman; (5) Main covariate-adjusted OLS (sex, age, race dummies, log family income with missing indicator, education) with HC1 SEs; (6) Six sensitivity analyses (ordinal, continuous, logistic obesity endpoint, ASVAB covariate, winsorized BMI, alternative corrupted-height BMI). Executed code: analysis.py; full output: analysis_output.txt.

payload.hypothesis: Weak positive association only, not causal: individuals with more present-oriented (net-withdrawing) saving behavior in 1989 had higher baseline BMI in 1981 (+0.28 kg/m2, 95% CI 0.10-0.46, covariate-adjusted; monotonic across all four savings categories; robust to ordinal/continuous operationalizations, winsorization, and cognitive covariate; not significant for BMI>=30). Because BMI predates the savings measure, reverse causation cannot be ruled out.
payload.workflow: QC (units: weights=pounds, H1985=inches, H1981 corrupted; missingness; outliers) -> BMI from W1981+H1985 (n=10,573) -> time preference proxy: binary withdrawal-vs-deposit (n=5,469), 4-level ordinal, signed log net savings -> descriptive + univariate tests -> main OLS with sex/age/race/income/education -> 6 sensitivity analyses. Artifacts: analysis.py, analysis_output.txt.
